name: Mandelic acid

card.summary: A larger, slower-penetrating alpha-hydroxy acid used in gentle peels and serums for acne and dark spots; direct clinical evidence is thin.
card.aka: Alpha-hydroxy phenylacetic acid, AHA, mandelic peel
card.note: Studied mostly as part of formulations or in broader AHA reviews; few dedicated trials of mandelic acid alone.

quick.overview:
Mandelic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA) used in skincare as a chemical exfoliant, mainly for acne, uneven pigmentation and sensitive skin. It is sold in serums and professional-strength peels.

A large Cochrane review covered AHA treatments for acne as a class. Dedicated mandelic acid trials are limited in the available literature; registered trials compare mandelic peels with tranexamic acid for melasma and test a combined peel for periocular rejuvenation.
quick.mechanism: Mandelic acid is described as having a larger molecular size than glycolic acid, which is said to slow skin penetration and reduce irritation. As an AHA it promotes exfoliation and cell turnover, and encyclopedic summaries describe antibacterial activity.
quick.risks: Common AHA effects are stinging, redness and peeling. The published literature give little mandelic acid-specific safety data. It has been studied as a natural preservative in emulsions, and sun protection is generally advised with AHA products.

lead: Mandelic acid (2-hydroxy-2-phenylacetic acid, C8H8O3) is an aromatic alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA) first isolated from bitter almonds. In skincare it is used as a chemical exfoliant in serums and superficial peels, aimed at acne-prone skin, uneven pigmentation and early signs of photoaging: it loosens the dead surface layer so skin looks smoother and more even.[9][1]

Its molecule is larger than glycolic or lactic acid, and an AI-generated encyclopedic summary says it therefore penetrates skin more slowly and causes less irritation, an attribute that makes it popular for sensitive or darker skin.[1] That summary also cites formulation studies reporting acne lesion reductions of up to 69 percent; its citations were not independently verified.[1]

Controlled clinical evidence specific to mandelic acid is limited. A Cochrane review assessed topical AHAs for acne as a group, a 2025 clinical study tested a cream containing mandelic acid and Centella asiatica in aging skin, and registered trials are examining mandelic peels in melasma and in a periocular peel.[3][10][6][7]

paras: Cosmetic uses include chemical peels and serums for acne-prone, pigmented or photoaged skin, with exfoliation attributed to the acid's effect on cell turnover.[1] Wikipedia describes mandelic acid peels as belonging to the superficial peel class.[9] The slower penetration of its larger molecule is the usual reason given for choosing it when other AHAs sting or redden the skin.[1]

Mandelic acid also appears in combination products. A 12-week single-centre study in 41 adults aged 40 to 75 with sensitive skin and photodamage tested a cream containing mandelic acid and Centella asiatica twice daily on the neck and limbs, and reported significant improvements in crepiness, texture, thickness and overall appearance, with improved dryness and scaling and no other measurable tolerability changes.[10] Because the cream contained more than one active ingredient, that result is not specific to mandelic acid alone.

Beyond skincare, mandelic acid is an important precursor in organic synthesis: Wikipedia notes that homatropine is an ester of mandelic acid and that cefamandole was also synthesised from it.[9] It has also been studied as a natural preservative; a 2024 paper examined emulsions formulated with mandelic acid and essential oils as sustainable preservatives.[5]

Mandelic acid is a white crystalline solid, soluble in water and polar organic solvents, with a pKa of 3.41. The molecule is chiral, and the racemic mixture is called paramandelic acid.[9] It is usually prepared by acid-catalysed hydrolysis of mandelonitrile, the cyanohydrin of benzaldehyde, and the enzyme mandelate racemase interconverts its enantiomers in the biological mandelate pathway.[9]

The German pharmacist Ferdinand Ludwig Winckler discovered mandelic acid in 1831 while heating amygdalin, an extract of bitter almonds, with dilute hydrochloric acid, and the name comes from the German word for almond.[9] Wikipedia also notes that it is among early pharmaceutical cocrystal examples studied by Higuchi and colleagues in the 1950s.[9] Its adoption in chemical peels and serums is documented mainly through product literature and cosmetic-dermatology practice rather than a single traceable origin.

Mandelic acid belongs to the alpha-hydroxy acid family alongside glycolic, lactic and citric acid, whose shared cosmetic role is chemical exfoliation of the skin surface.[11] The US FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel regard AHAs as safe at low concentrations and at a pH above about 3.5 when used with sun-protection instructions, and the FDA has warned consumers that AHAs can raise sunburn likelihood, an effect that reverses once use stops.[11] Mild irritation, redness and flaking are the most common side effects across the class.[11]

Within the class, mandelic acid is chosen in cosmetic dermatology mainly for its size: with a larger molecule than glycolic acid, it penetrates more slowly, which practitioners cite as the reason it irritates less and is often offered to people with sensitive skin or darker skin tones prone to post-inflammatory marks.[1] That tolerability rationale is a mechanism-based explanation that the product literature and dermatology practice rely on.[1]

A 2020 Cochrane review of topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and alpha-hydroxy acids for acne included 49 randomised trials with 3,880 participants, mostly with mild to moderate acne, and examined patient self-assessment, withdrawals, minor adverse events and quality of life; mandelic acid was not the review's sole subject, and the authors rated evidence for many comparisons as low or very low quality.[3] A 2022 network meta-analysis of acne treatments covers other topical and oral options.[2]

A registered trial of 120 participants (not yet recruiting) plans to compare intralesional tranexamic acid with a mandelic acid peel for melasma.[6] A completed phase IV registration of 12 participants evaluated a duosomal chemical peel for aesthetic enhancement of periocular and facial regions.[7] A randomised trial of a peel formulated with polyhydroxy acids across skin types, including sensitive skin, concerns a different acid class.[4] No large randomised trial of mandelic acid alone for acne or pigmentation has been published.

A 2019 study in the Journal of the Pakistan Association of Dermatologists compared a 30 percent salicylic acid peel with a 20 percent salicylic plus 10 percent mandelic acid combination peel in 50 patients with acne, 41 of whom completed four sessions. Reduction in active lesions was greater with the salicylic acid peel, while post-acne melanosis (leftover dark marks) fell more with the combination peel, and the authors described both as well tolerated.[12] Because mandelic acid was part of a mixture, the study speaks to the combination and not to the acid alone.

Encyclopedic summaries describe mandelic acid as gentler than smaller AHAs.[1] Wikipedia lists it as moderately toxic if ingested and notes that urinary mandelic acid is a standard biomarker for styrene and ethylbenzene exposure in occupational medicine.[9] No safety trial specific to mandelic acid in cosmetic use has been published.

Wikipedia reports that a 2025 Delphi consensus study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology did not recommend mandelic acid for acne, citing cost and insurance coverage relative to vitamin A derivatives.[9]

A 2005 T Nation thread on fighting acne includes one user's report that a mandelic acid lotion helped their acne over a few years.[8] This is an individual anecdote and the topic appears only occasionally in looksmaxxing forums.

timeline.event: Ferdinand Ludwig Winckler discovers mandelic acid from bitter almond extract.[9]
Cochrane review of topical agents including AHAs for acne published.[3]
Clinical study of a mandelic acid and Centella cream in aging skin published.[10]

lore.intro: Mandelic acid comes up occasionally in skin-focused discussions as a gentle exfoliant.[8]

claims.claim: Mandelic acid lotion can clear stubborn acne
claims.believers: A 2005 T Nation poster said a mandelic acid lotion seemed to help acne a lot after a few years of breakouts.[8]
claims.experts: Controlled evidence specific to mandelic acid is limited; the Cochrane review examined topical AHAs for acne as a group and rated many comparisons as low-quality evidence.[3]

claims.claim: Its larger molecule makes it gentler than glycolic acid
claims.believers: Skincare discussions say mandelic acid penetrates more slowly, so it stings less.[1]
claims.experts: The claim comes from encyclopedic and product-literature summaries; no head-to-head irritation trial in the cited literature compares mandelic with glycolic acid.[1]

chain: Exfoliates the outer layer of dead skin cells
Smoother texture and fewer clogged pores
angle.text: Used as a peel or leave-on serum, mandelic acid sheds the outer skin layer, which can smooth texture and help with breakouts and uneven tone. People favour it as a milder alternative to smaller AHAs, particularly for sensitive skin.
